title: Fitting stair spindles into a bottom tread
subtitle: Fit replacement balusters between the handrail above and the tread below by drilling angled holes in the tread and seating each spindle firmly
excerpt: How to fit stair spindles (balusters) between the handrail and the stair tread. Covers setting out spindle positions, drilling angled holes in the tread, cutting spindles to length, and securing top and bottom ends.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK Building Regulations Part K and trade joinery practice for staircase balustrades.

glossaryTerms.definition: The individual vertical member in a balustrade that runs from the handrail down to the string or tread below. Also called a spindle or stair rod. Balusters are spaced at centres that prevent a 100 mm sphere from passing between them (the UK Building Regulations requirement), protecting against children falling or trapping their heads.

The full assembly of handrail, balusters, and lower fixing at the edge of a staircase. The balustrade prevents falls from the open side of the stair and must be capable of withstanding a horizontal force of at least 0.74 kN/m under UK Building Regulations.

content.text: Stair spindles run from the underside of the handrail down through the tread or base rail. Where spindles are housed directly in the tread, each joint must be accurate and tight to prevent rattle and movement. INTERMEDIATE: drilling on an angle and fitting into a staircase that is not always perfectly plumb takes care and test-fitting.

positions on the tread, spacing them so that no gap between spindles exceeds 100 mm. Two spindles per tread is typical on a domestic stair. Measure the gap width and divide evenly. Mark the centre of each hole on the tread at the same position relative to the front edge of the tread.
Drill the tread holes at the correct angle

The holes in the tread must match the pitch angle of the staircase. Set a sliding bevel to the stair pitch angle by holding it against the string (the diagonal side board). Drill the holes in the tread at this angle using a flat or auger bit sized to match the spindle base diameter, typically 18 to 20 mm. Keep the drill at the bevel angle throughout and drill to the housing depth marked on the bit with tape.
Measure and cut each spindle to length

Measure from the bottom of the hole in the tread to the underside of the handrail at the spindle position. The spindle must be cut with both ends squared or angled to match the tread and handrail angles. Cut one end square and test the fit; adjust for the angle at the top where the spindle seats into the handrail housing or flat against its underside.

Apply a small amount of wood glue in the tread hole and at the handrail fixing point. Insert the spindle into the tread hole and tap gently with the rubber mallet to seat the base. At the top, glue or pin the spindle to the handrail according to the fixing type: dowel housing, rebate, or a face-fixed pin through the rail into the spindle end. Check the
is plumb by eye before the glue sets.

attrs.symptom: Spindle rattles in the tread hole after fixing
attrs.cause: The hole was drilled oversize for the spindle diameter, or the spindle was not glued into the housing.
attrs.fix: Remove the spindle, clean out the hole, and apply a fresh bead of PVA glue. Pack the gap with a thin sliver of matching timber if the gap is significant before re-gluing.

attrs.symptom: Spindle leans out of plumb when the glue sets
attrs.cause: The hole angle did not exactly match the stair pitch, or the handrail housing was not aligned with the tread hole.
attrs.fix: The lean will be small and often acceptable. For a significant lean, remove and re-drill at the correct angle before re-fitting.
